reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Results from disruption of the vagus or recurrent laryngeal nerve supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, and may be unilateral or bilateral
Unilateral palsy typically causes a breathy, weak voice and sometimes aspiration, as the healthy cord may compensate over time
Bilateral palsy is more dangerous: the cords may sit near the midline, threatening the airway and causing stridor
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a longer intrathoracic course, making it more vulnerable to chest pathology such as mediastinal or lung disease
Common causes include surgical injury (notably thyroid surgery), malignancy along the nerve's course, and neurological or idiopathic causes
A thorough search for the cause is essential, examining the neck, thyroid, chest and skull base along the nerve pathway
Management principles include voice therapy, treating the underlying cause, and procedures such as injection or medialisation to improve glottic closure
In bilateral palsy with airway compromise, securing the airway takes priority, sometimes requiring tracheostomy
reference.pathophysiology: Vocal cord palsy arises from interruption anywhere along the motor pathway to the larynx, from the brainstem nucleus through the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Loss of innervation impairs abduction and adduction of the affected fold, so it rests in a position determined by the residual muscle tone and any compensatory changes. The recurrent laryngeal nerve's long course, especially on the left where it loops under the aortic arch, exposes it to compression or invasion by neck and chest disease and to iatrogenic injury during surgery. The functional consequence depends on the resting position of the cords and whether one or both are affected.
additionalDifferentials: Cricoarytenoid joint fixation (e.g. from arthritis or trauma)
Vocal fold nodules, polyps or scarring
additionalInvestigations: Laryngoscopy to confirm reduced or absent cord movement and assess position
CT or MRI along the course of the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves from skull base to chest
Chest imaging to exclude thoracic causes
Thyroid and neck evaluation, including relevant surgical history
Neurological assessment and laryngeal electromyography in selected cases
redFlags: Bilateral palsy with stridor or respiratory distress requiring urgent airway management
Progressive symptoms with a neck mass, weight loss or haemoptysis suggesting malignancy
Aspiration with recurrent chest infections from poor glottic closure
Associated cranial nerve deficits pointing to a skull base or brainstem lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause and whether the palsy is unilateral or bilateral; some idiopathic or postviral unilateral palsies recover, others compensate with voice therapy, while bilateral palsy often needs airway intervention and malignant causes carry the outlook of the underlying disease.
pitfalls: Labelling a palsy idiopathic without imaging the entire nerve pathway to exclude a tumour
Underestimating airway risk in bilateral palsy
Missing silent aspiration in patients with poor glottic closure
Confusing cricoarytenoid joint fixation or cancer with a neurogenic palsy
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
